title: Training stability at scale
summary: Diagnose and fix real training failures: NaN gradients, dead neurons, learning-rate thrashing. Reproduce a small scaling-law experiment. The capstone for ML engineers moving from 'I trained a model' to 'I shipped a model that actually trains.'
contentIntro:
## What you'll build

A training-instrumentation toolkit + a series of experiments where you deliberately break a training run and bring it back. By the end you'll have a notebook that:

- Logs loss + gradient norms + activation magnitudes per step
- Reproduces a small scaling-law experiment
- Recovers from at least 3 failure modes (NaN gradient, dead neurons, LR thrashing)

The capstone signals to employers that you can run training experiments responsibly — not just launch and hope.

contentUndergrad:
## What you'll build

Four milestones, ~4 weeks. Each milestone is a notebook + a writeup of what you observed. The model is small (a 100M-parameter transformer is plenty) — the value is in the methodology, not the scale.

## Format

You need a single GPU (16GB+). Cloud is fine. The lessons aren't about scale-up; they're about diagnostic discipline that transfers to any scale.

contentGrad:
## What you'll build

A training-discipline toolkit you'd hand to a junior engineer to use. Defense (claim-thread Q&A on the artifact page) covers: why training instabilities arise, what each diagnostic signal indicates, and how the recipe choices in modern open models (mixed precision, grad clipping, warmup) were arrived at empirically.

milestones.title: Instrument the training loop
milestones.description:
Build a training script that logs:

- Train loss + held-out val loss per epoch (and per N steps)
- Gradient norm per step (clip at 1.0 by default; log the pre-clip norm)
- Per-layer gradient norms (so you can spot vanishing/exploding gradients)
- Activation statistics (mean + std of activations at each layer)
- Learning rate per step (verify the schedule is doing what you expected)

Use Weights & Biases, TensorBoard, or even matplotlib + JSON logs. Pick a small architecture (100M-parameter transformer is plenty) and a small dataset (tinystories, code samples, anything stable).

In your writeup: a single dashboard image showing all your signals during a healthy run. Annotate what each signal looks like in the steady-state.

criteria.aiPrompt: Score whether the instrumentation captures train+val loss, gradient norms (pre-clip + per-layer), activation statistics, and LR schedule. Is the dashboard readable?
Score the annotation depth: does the learner identify what each signal looks like in healthy training?
Score whether the script + config are reproducible by another engineer.

milestones.title: Recover from three failure modes
milestones.description:
Deliberately break the training run in three specific ways. For each: identify the failure from your instrumentation; explain what happened; show the fix.

**1. NaN gradient**: train at LR 5× too high (or remove gradient clipping with a noisy minibatch). Show the run NaNs. Identify the diagnostic signature (gradient norm spikes before the NaN). Show the fix (lower LR + enable clipping).

**2. Dead neurons**: use ReLU with bad init (positive bias). Run for a few epochs. Show that some neurons never activate. Identify them in your activation logs. Apply the fix (Kaiming init, or switch to GELU/SwiGLU).

**3. LR thrashing**: pick a schedule that's too aggressive (cosine to a high LR after a short warmup). Show the loss bouncing around without converging. Show the fix (longer warmup, gentler schedule).

In your writeup: three before/after dashboards with annotations. The grader scores on diagnostic depth, not just whether you fixed it.

criteria.description: Each failure mode is diagnosed from the instrumentation, not just observed.
criteria.aiPrompt: Score whether the learner identifies each failure mode from specific signals (gradient norm spike, dead-neuron activation profile, LR thrashing pattern), not just from external behavior.
Score whether the proposed fixes actually fix the failures, with evidence in the dashboard.
Score the writeup's clarity in showing before/after comparisons.

milestones.title: Reproduce a small scaling-law experiment
milestones.description:
Train your small model at three sizes (e.g., 30M, 100M, 300M params) on the same dataset for the same number of tokens. Plot loss vs parameter count on a log-log scale.

You should see a power-law relationship — small loss differences but consistent shape. Fit a curve to the points. Compare your fitted exponent to the Kaplan / Chinchilla literature (it'll likely be different because your dataset and recipe are different — that's the point).

In your writeup: the log-log plot, the fitted exponent, and a discussion of why your number differs from the literature (LR schedule, data quality, model size range, etc.).

This milestone is about building empirical intuition for scaling laws — that they're recipe-dependent, not universal constants.

criteria.description: Three model sizes trained correctly with comparable settings.
criteria.aiPrompt: Score whether the three runs are properly controlled (same data, same token count, same recipe except for model size).
Score the rigor of the scaling-law analysis. Is the fit reasonable? Does the discussion engage with why the exponent differs from published values?
Score the plot's readability and the writeup's depth on what scaling laws do and don't tell you.

milestones.title: Propose and validate one optimization
milestones.description:
Pick one optimization from this list (or another you can defend):

- **Mixed precision (bf16 or fp16)**: implement it; measure speedup + memory savings; report any quality delta
- **Gradient accumulation**: enable it; verify effective batch size scales as expected; report any training-dynamics differences
- **Cosine LR schedule with warmup**: replace the default linear schedule; measure final-loss difference at fixed compute
- **Gradient checkpointing**: enable it; measure activation-memory savings + step-time overhead
- **Compiled model (torch.compile)**: apply it; measure step-time speedup + any compatibility issues

In your writeup: explain the optimization, show the before/after measurements, discuss any tradeoffs you found. Include at least one *negative result* — something you tried that didn't help.

The scoring rewards engineering judgment. A clean negative result is as good as a clean positive result.

criteria.aiPrompt: Score whether the optimization is correctly implemented and the measurements are meaningful (right metric, fair comparison, sensible scale).
Score the depth of the tradeoff discussion. Does the learner identify both the wins and the costs? Is the negative result substantive?
Score the final engineering judgment: would the learner ship this optimization in production? Why or why not?
